Contents.Title: Introduction: Now We Build the POS System
Contents.Contents:
From Authentication to the Application

We have now built both sides of our basic authentication system.

Users can create accounts with Sign Up, and existing users can use Login to enter the application.

But logging in should eventually lead somewhere.

Right now, our project can authenticate the user, but we have not yet built the main application that appears after Login.

This Is Where the POS System Comes In

Our project will now grow from an authentication example into a simple Point of Sale, or POS, system.

A POS system is an application used to select products, build an order, calculate prices, receive payment, and produce a receipt.

For our learning project, we will build a simplified version.

What We Are Going to Build

Login
↓
Successful authentication
↓
Open the POS application

POS
├── Products
├── Current Order
├── Quantity controls
├── Subtotal
├── Tax
├── Total
├── Money Received
├── Change
├── Clear
├── Print
└── Checkout

Three Technologies Again

HTML
↓
Creates the POS structure

CSS
↓
Designs the POS interface

JavaScript
↓
Makes the POS interactive

This means we are returning to the same learning pattern we used for Sign-In and Sign-Up.

First we create the structure, then we style it, and finally we add behavior.

The Important Connection With Login

Our Login code already has a successful branch.

Previously, that branch only displayed a success message.

Now we need to modify it so a successful Login also opens the POS application.

In our project, the POS container is:

<div id="posApp">
  ...
</div>

And the authentication overlay is:

<div class="auth-overlay" id="authOverlay">
  ...
</div>

The successful Login flow will eventually become:

Login succeeds
↓
Hide authOverlay
↓
Show posApp
↓
User enters the POS system

Why Are We Learning This Now?

Because the project is becoming a real application instead of a collection of unrelated examples.

We are going to reuse the concepts you already learned:

  • HTML elements and IDs
  • CSS classes
  • JavaScript variables
  • arrays and objects
  • events
  • conditions
  • DOM manipulation

Try It

Continue using the same project. Do not create a separate website for the POS. The goal is to make the POS become the application that appears after a successful Login.

Contents.Title: HTML: Start the POS Application
Contents.Contents:
We Need a Container for the POS

Before creating products, carts, or buttons, we need a place where the POS interface can live.

Our authentication system already has a main overlay and card. The POS will exist separately from that authentication area.

We can create a main container:

<div id="posApp">
</div>

Why Give It an ID?

We already learned that an ID gives JavaScript a way to find a specific element.

Later, after Login succeeds, JavaScript will need to find the POS container and show it.

document.getElementById("posApp")

This gives JavaScript access to the POS application element.

The Relationship With Authentication

Authentication
↓
id="authOverlay"

POS
↓
id="posApp"

We now have two major parts of the application.

Try It

Add the posApp container to the same HTML document you used for Sign-In and Sign-Up. For now, leave it empty and make sure you understand that it is the container for the application that will appear after Login.

Contents.Title: HTML: Create the POS Layout
Contents.Contents:
Divide the POS Into Two Main Areas

A POS interface needs more than one section.

We can divide our application into two main areas:

Left
↓
Products

Right
↓
Current Order

HTML gives us the <main> element for the main content of the application and the <section> element for related groups of content.

Our structure can begin like this:

<div id="posApp">

  <main class="pos">

    <section class="panel">
      Products
    </section>

    <section class="panel">
      Current Order
    </section>

  </main>

</div>

Why Use Two Sections?

The left side will be responsible for displaying available products.

The right side will be responsible for displaying the current order and payment information.

This separation makes the interface easier to understand and style.

What Is class="panel"?

We can give both sections the same class:

class="panel"

Because the class is reusable, CSS can later style both sections using one rule.

Try It

Create the two main POS sections inside posApp. Give both sections the panel class. Do not worry about making them look good yet. We are still building the HTML structure.

Contents.Title: HTML: Build the Products Section
Contents.Contents:
Now Create the Product Area

The first half of the POS is where the available products will appear.

We can give the section a heading and supporting text.

<header class="header">
  <h1>Products</h1>
  <p>Choose a product</p>
</header>

Why Use header?

The <header> element represents introductory content for a section or part of a page.

In this case, it contains the title and explanation for the product area.

Now Add a Body Area

<div class="body">

</div>

This gives us another container where the actual products can be placed.

The Product Container

We can then create:

<div
  class="products"
  id="products"
></div>

This element will eventually contain the product buttons created by JavaScript.

Why Does It Need an ID?

JavaScript will eventually need to find this container so it can create product elements inside it.

document.getElementById("products")

Our Structure So Far

Products panel
├── Header
│   ├── Products
│   └── Choose a product
│
└── Body
    └── Products container

Try It

Build the Products section using the structure shown above. Keep the id="products" exactly as shown because JavaScript will use that ID later.

Contents.Title: HTML: Build the Current Order Section
Contents.Contents:
Now Create the Order Area

The second half of the POS will show what the customer has selected.

We can use the same header structure:

<header class="header">
  <h1>Current Order</h1>
  <p>Your selected products</p>
</header>

Then we create a body:

<div class="body">

</div>

The Cart Is a Table

A POS order naturally fits a table because each item can have several pieces of information.

For example:

Name
Price
Quantity
Total

We can begin with:

<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th>Name</th>
      <th>Price</th>
      <th>Qty</th>
      <th>Total</th>
      <th></th>
    </tr>
  </thead>

  <tbody id="cart">
  </tbody>
</table>

Why Does tbody Have an ID?

JavaScript will later create and remove order rows inside the <tbody>.

document.getElementById("cart")

The table structure is written in HTML, while JavaScript will control the changing order data.

Try It

Create the Current Order section and its table. Make sure the table contains the headings Name, Price, Qty, and Total, plus an empty final heading for the remove button.

Contents.Title: HTML: Add the POS Totals
Contents.Contents:
Calculate the Cost of the Order

A POS needs to show more than the list of products. It also needs to calculate the money involved in the order.

We need three main totals:

Subtotal
Tax
Total

We can create a summary section:

<div class="summary">

  <div class="row">
    <span>Subtotal</span>
    <strong id="subtotal">₱0.00</strong>
  </div>

  <div class="row">
    <span>Tax</span>
    <strong id="tax">₱0.00</strong>
  </div>

  <div class="row total">
    <span>Total</span>
    <strong id="total">₱0.00</strong>
  </div>

</div>

Why Do These Elements Need IDs?

JavaScript will eventually calculate the values and replace the text inside these elements.

subtotal
↓
id="subtotal"

Tax
↓
id="tax"

Total
↓
id="total"

This is another example of HTML providing the structure and JavaScript later providing the changing values.

Try It

Add the three summary rows to your Current Order section. Keep the IDs exactly as shown because the JavaScript lesson will use them later.

Contents.Title: HTML: Add Payment and Change
Contents.Contents:
Let the Customer Enter Money

The POS now has an order and totals, but we still need a way to enter the amount of money received.

We can create a payment section:

<div class="payment">

  <label for="money">
    Money Received
  </label>

  <input
    id="money"
    type="number"
    min="0"
    placeholder="Enter amount"
  >

</div>

Why type="number"?

The amount is numerical, so the number input type is appropriate.

Why min="0"?

A received payment should not normally be negative, so the minimum value is set to zero.

Now Show Change

<div class="change">
  <span>Change</span>
  <strong id="change">₱0.00</strong>
</div>

The change value will be calculated by JavaScript.

The Basic Calculation

Money Received
−
Total
=
Change

Try It

Add the Money Received input and Change display. Make sure the input has id="money" and the change display has id="change".

Contents.Title: HTML: Add the POS Action Buttons
Contents.Contents:
Give the User Controls

The POS needs actions that allow the user to work with the current order.

We need:

Clear
Print
Checkout

We can create them like this:

<div class="actions">

  <button
    class="action"
    id="clear"
    type="button"
  >
    Clear
  </button>

  <button
    class="action"
    id="print"
    type="button"
  >
    Print
  </button>

  <button
    class="action checkout"
    id="checkout"
    type="button"
  >
    Checkout
  </button>

</div>

Why type="button"?

These buttons are not submitting the Login or Sign-Up forms. They are normal application controls, so we explicitly use type="button".

Why Give Each Button an ID?

JavaScript will later attach click events to these exact buttons.

clear
print
checkout

Primary and Secondary Actions

The Checkout button is the main action, while Clear and Print are supporting actions.

That difference will later be reflected in the CSS.

Try It

Add the three action buttons. Do not add JavaScript yet. Clicking them does not need to do anything at this stage because we are still building the HTML.

Contents.Title: HTML: Add the Receipt Area
Contents.Contents:
The POS Should Be Able to Show a Receipt

After processing an order, the application should be able to generate a readable receipt.

We can use a <textarea> to display the receipt.

<div class="receipt-section">

  <label for="receipt">
    Receipt
  </label>

  <textarea
    id="receipt"
    readonly
    placeholder="Click Print to generate the receipt..."
  ></textarea>

</div>

Why textarea?

A receipt contains multiple lines of text, so a multi-line element makes sense.

Why readonly?

The receipt is generated by the application. The user should not manually edit the generated receipt through this field.

Why Does It Have an ID?

JavaScript will later place the generated receipt text into it:

document.getElementById("receipt")

Try It

Add the receipt section and textarea. At this point, your HTML should contain the full structural pieces of the POS system even though it is not styled or functional yet.

Contents.Title: HTML: Complete the POS Structure
Contents.Contents:
Put the Whole POS Together

We have now created the individual HTML pieces.

The overall structure should look roughly like this:

<div id="posApp">

  <main class="pos">

    <section class="panel">

      <header class="header">
        <h1>Products</h1>
        <p>Choose a product</p>
      </header>

      <div class="body">
        <div class="products" id="products"></div>
      </div>

    </section>

    <section class="panel">

      <header class="header">
        <h1>Current Order</h1>
        <p>Your selected products</p>
      </header>

      <div class="body">

        <div class="cart">
          <table>
            ...
            <tbody id="cart"></tbody>
          </table>
        </div>

        <div class="summary">
          ...
        </div>

      </div>

    </section>

  </main>

</div>

What Have We Created?

POS
├── Product area
├── Current order
├── Cart table
├── Subtotal
├── Tax
├── Total
├── Money received
├── Change
├── Clear
├── Print
├── Checkout
└── Receipt

There is still no behavior. That is intentional.

HTML answers the first question:

What exists?

We will answer the next question with CSS:

How does it look?

Try It

Make sure your POS HTML structure is complete before moving to CSS. You should be able to see all of the sections in the browser even though they may look plain.

Contents.Title: CSS: Begin Styling the POS
Contents.Contents:
HTML Exists — Now We Need Design

The POS structure is now present, but the browser is displaying it using mostly default styles.

We already learned that CSS controls appearance.

Our POS will use the same visual language as the authentication interface:

Dark background
↓
Panels
↓
Rounded corners
↓
Subtle borders
↓
Blue accent
↓
Readable spacing

The POS Container

We can start by styling the main POS wrapper:

#posApp {
  display: none;
}

#posApp.show {
  display: block;
}

This is important because the POS should not appear before the user successfully logs in.

What Does This Mean?

Normally:

#posApp
↓
display: none
↓
POS is hidden

When JavaScript adds the show class:

#posApp.show
↓
display: block
↓
POS becomes visible

This is the CSS part of the Login-to-POS connection.

Try It

Add the #posApp and #posApp.show rules. Temporarily add the show class manually in your HTML to see how the visibility changes.

Contents.Title: CSS: Create the POS Grid
Contents.Contents:
Place Products Beside the Current Order

Our POS has two main panels, so a two-column layout is a good fit.

We can use CSS Grid:

.pos {
  width: 100%;
  max-width: 1400px;
  margin: auto;
  padding: 18px;

  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 1.2fr 1fr;
  gap: 18px;
}

display: grid

This activates CSS Grid, a layout system designed for rows and columns.

grid-template-columns

grid-template-columns: 1.2fr 1fr;

This creates two columns.

The first receives slightly more available space than the second.

gap

gap: 18px creates space between the two panels.

max-width

The POS should not become excessively wide on very large screens, so we give it a maximum width.

margin: auto

This helps center the POS within the available page width.

Try It

Apply the Grid layout to your POS. Experiment with 1fr 1fr and 2fr 1fr. Observe how the two panels change size.

Contents.Title: CSS: Style the POS Panels
Contents.Contents:
Turn the Sections Into Panels

We created the reusable panel class in HTML.

Now CSS can style both sections with one rule.

.panel {
  background: #171a21;
  border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.1);
  border-radius: 16px;
  overflow: hidden;
  box-shadow: 0 15px 40px rgba(0,0,0,.25);
}

Why Use a Shared Class?

Both the Products and Current Order sections should look like parts of the same application.

One class lets us apply the same style to both.

overflow: hidden

This keeps content from visually escaping the rounded panel edges.

Why Use box-shadow?

The shadow separates the panels from the dark page background.

Remember that this is a design choice. The panel would still work without it.

Try It

Add the panel rule and experiment with the border radius, border opacity, and shadow values.

Contents.Title: CSS: Style the POS Headers and Bodies
Contents.Contents:
Organize the Content Inside Each Panel

Each POS panel contains a header followed by its body.

We can create shared rules:

.header {
  padding: 16px;
  border-bottom: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.1);
}

.body {
  padding: 15px;
}

Header

The header needs separation from the main content underneath it.

The bottom border provides that visual separation.

Body

The body needs internal spacing so its contents do not touch the panel edges.

Style the Header Text

.header h1 {
  margin: 0;
  font-size: 1.2rem;
}

.header p {
  margin: 4px 0 0;
  color: #a9b0c0;
  font-size: .85rem;
}

The heading is stronger while the supporting paragraph is muted.

Try It

Style both POS headers and their body areas. Change the heading size and the spacing to see how the hierarchy changes.

Contents.Title: CSS: Create the Product Grid
Contents.Contents:
Make the Products Easy to Browse

The Products area will contain many product cards, so Grid is useful again.

.products {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(5, minmax(0, 1fr));
  gap: 10px;
}

repeat()

repeat(5, ...) tells CSS to create five columns using the same sizing rule.

Why minmax(0, 1fr)?

This allows each column to share the available space while avoiding unwanted minimum sizing behavior.

Product Cards

.product {
  min-width: 0;
  padding: 12px 8px;
  border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.1);
  border-radius: 12px;
  background: #1d2230;
  color: #e8eaf0;
  text-align: center;
}

Each product becomes its own small panel.

Product Name and Price

.product-name {
  font-weight: 800;
  font-size: .9rem;
}

.product-price {
  margin: 6px 0 10px;
  color: #8bd3ff;
  font-size: .85rem;
  font-weight: 700;
}

The product name gets emphasis while the price gets the accent-like color.

Try It

Build the product grid and product styles. Experiment with the number of columns and the gap between products.

Contents.Title: CSS: Style the Buy Button
Contents.Contents:
Give Every Product an Action

Each product needs a way for the user to add it to the order.

We will use the buy class.

.buy {
  width: 100%;
  padding: 7px 4px;
  border: 0;
  border-radius: 8px;
  background: #6ea8fe;
  color: #07111f;
  font-weight: 800;
  cursor: pointer;
}

Why width: 100%?

The button should fill the available width of its product card.

Why cursor: pointer?

It communicates that the button is interactive.

Hover

.buy:hover {
  filter: brightness(1.1);
}

This gives the button a small visual response when the pointer moves over it.

Try It

Style the Buy button and experiment with the background color, radius, padding, and hover brightness.

Contents.Title: CSS: Style the Cart Table
Contents.Contents:
Make the Current Order Readable

The cart is a table, so we need spacing and borders that make each row understandable.

.cart {
  width: 100%;
  overflow-x: auto;
  border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.1);
  border-radius: 11px;
}

table {
  width: 100%;
  border-collapse: collapse;
  min-width: 430px;
}

Why overflow-x?

The table contains several columns. On a narrow device it may not fit comfortably, so horizontal scrolling gives it room without breaking the rest of the page.

Style Table Cells

th,
td {
  padding: 9px;
  border-bottom: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.1);
  text-align: left;
  font-size: .84rem;
}

Style Headers

th {
  background: rgba(255,255,255,.04);
  color: #a9b0c0;
}

Empty Cart

.empty {
  padding: 25px;
  text-align: center;
  color: #a9b0c0;
}

This gives the user a readable message when there are no items.

Try It

Apply the table styling. Experiment with padding, border opacity, font size, and the minimum table width.

Contents.Title: CSS: Style Quantity Controls
Contents.Contents:
Control How Many Items Are Ordered

The cart will allow the user to increase or decrease the quantity of a product.

We can group those controls with:

.quantity {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 5px;
}

Then style the buttons:

.quantity button {
  width: 26px;
  height: 26px;
  padding: 0;
  border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.1);
  border-radius: 6px;
  background: #22283a;
  color: #e8eaf0;
  cursor: pointer;
}

The Quantity Number

.quantity span {
  min-width: 20px;
  text-align: center;
}

The controls become:

−   2   +

The minus and plus buttons will later be connected to JavaScript.

Try It

Style the quantity controls and experiment with their dimensions and spacing.

Contents.Title: CSS: Style Totals and Payment
Contents.Contents:
Make the Money Information Easy to Read

The order summary should clearly distinguish normal information from the important final total.

Start with:

.summary {
  margin-top: 15px;
  padding-top: 12px;
  border-top: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.1);
}

Summary Rows

.row {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: space-between;
  padding: 5px 0;
  color: #a9b0c0;
}

.row strong {
  color: #e8eaf0;
}

Highlight the Total

.total {
  margin-top: 6px;
  padding-top: 10px;
  border-top: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.1);
  font-size: 1.2rem;
}

.total strong {
  color: #6ea8fe;
}

Money Input

.payment {
  margin-top: 12px;
}

.payment input {
  width: 100%;
  padding: 10px;
  border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.1);
  border-radius: 9px;
  background: #1d2230;
  color: #e8eaf0;
  font: inherit;
}

Change

.change {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: space-between;
  margin-top: 9px;
  padding: 10px;
  border-radius: 9px;
  background: rgba(114,214,160,.08);
  border: 1px solid rgba(114,214,160,.15);
}

.change strong {
  color: #72d6a0;
}

Try It

Apply the summary, payment, and change styles. Experiment with the total font size and the change colors.

Contents.Title: CSS: Style the POS Buttons and Receipt
Contents.Contents:
Finish the Visual Layer

We have only a few visual pieces left.

Action Buttons

.actions {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr;
  gap: 8px;
  margin-top: 12px;
}

.action {
  padding: 11px;
  border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.1);
  border-radius: 9px;
  background: #22283a;
  color: #e8eaf0;
  font-weight: 700;
  cursor: pointer;
}

Checkout

.checkout {
  grid-column: 1 / -1;
  background: #6ea8fe;
  color: #07111f;
  border-color: transparent;
}

The Checkout button spans both columns because it is the primary action.

Receipt

.receipt-section {
  margin-top: 15px;
}

#receipt {
  width: 100%;
  min-height: 190px;
  resize: vertical;
  padding: 12px;
  border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.1);
  border-radius: 10px;
  background: #10131a;
  color: #e8eaf0;
  font-family: monospace;
  font-size: .82rem;
  outline: none;
}

Remove Button

.remove {
  border: 0;
  background: none;
  color: #ff7f8a;
  font-size: 18px;
  cursor: pointer;
}

Try It

Finish the button, receipt, and remove-button styles. Compare the result with the authentication design you built earlier. Notice that the project now uses the same visual theme across different parts of the application.

Contents.Title: CSS: Make the POS Responsive
Contents.Contents:
The POS Must Work on Smaller Screens

Our two-column layout is useful on a large screen, but it may not fit comfortably on a phone.

We can use a media query:

@media (max-width: 1000px) {
  .pos {
    grid-template-columns: 1fr;
  }
}

When the screen becomes narrow enough, the two panels stack vertically.

What Changes?

Large screen

Products     Current Order

Small screen

Products

Current Order

Very Small Screens

For narrow devices, the product grid can become horizontally scrollable:

@media (max-width: 600px) {
  .pos {
    padding: 10px;
  }

  .products {
    grid-template-columns: repeat(5, 120px);
    overflow-x: auto;
    padding-bottom: 5px;
  }

  .product {
    width: 120px;
  }
}

This keeps the product cards usable without forcing everything into an extremely narrow column.

Try It

Test your POS at different screen sizes. Change the media-query breakpoints and observe when the layout switches from two columns to one.

Contents.Title: CSS: Our POS Design Is Finished
Contents.Contents:
Review the POS Design Layer

The POS now has its complete visual structure.

We used CSS to create:

  • a two-column application layout
  • reusable panels
  • headers and body areas
  • a product grid
  • product cards
  • buttons
  • a cart table
  • quantity controls
  • summary rows
  • payment controls
  • receipt styling
  • responsive behavior

The Same Separation We Used Before

HTML
↓
What exists?

CSS
↓
How does it look?

JavaScript
↓
What does it do?

The POS is still mostly static because JavaScript has not been added yet.

That is exactly what we want.

But There Is One More Important CSS Connection

The authentication and POS areas are designed to coexist in the same document.

Authentication
↓
Visible first

POS
↓
Hidden first

Then JavaScript will decide when the POS becomes visible.

Try It

Review your POS in the browser. Make sure the layout looks correct before starting the JavaScript lessons. Do not move the POS into a separate page. We will connect it directly to the Login system we already built.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Introduce the POS Data
Contents.Contents:
The POS Now Needs Data

The HTML and CSS give us the POS interface, but the product area is currently empty.

JavaScript needs some information to work with.

Luckily, we already learned about arrays and objects.

Remember the Pattern

Array
↓
Many items

Object
↓
Named information about one item

A product can be represented by an object:

{
  name: "Burger",
  price: 85
}

But the POS has many products, so we use an array of product objects.

const products = [
  {name: "Burger", price: 85},
  {name: "Pizza", price: 120},
  {name: "Fries", price: 55},
  {name: "Hotdog", price: 45},
  {name: "Chicken", price: 110}
];

Why Is This Perfect for the POS?

Each object describes one product.

The array stores all available products.

This is exactly the Array + Object combination we learned earlier.

The Cart Is Another Array

The current order will also contain multiple objects.

let cart = [];

Each item in the cart can contain:

name
price
quantity

Two Collections

products
↓
Available products

cart
↓
Currently selected products

Try It

Create a small products array containing at least five objects. Give every product a name and price. Then create an empty cart array.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Find the POS Elements
Contents.Contents:
Connect JavaScript to the POS HTML

Our POS HTML already contains IDs for the elements that need to change.

JavaScript can find them using getElementById().

const productsEl =
  document.getElementById("products");

const cartEl =
  document.getElementById("cart");

const subtotalEl =
  document.getElementById("subtotal");

const taxEl =
  document.getElementById("tax");

const totalEl =
  document.getElementById("total");

const moneyEl =
  document.getElementById("money");

const changeEl =
  document.getElementById("change");

const receiptEl =
  document.getElementById("receipt");

What Is Each Element For?

productsEl
↓
Where products appear

cartEl
↓
Where order rows appear

subtotalEl
↓
Subtotal display

taxEl
↓
Tax display

totalEl
↓
Total display

moneyEl
↓
Money received input

changeEl
↓
Change display

receiptEl
↓
Receipt output

This is the same HTML-to-JavaScript connection we learned with the Login form.

Try It

Find all of the POS elements using their IDs. Use console.log() while practicing to confirm that JavaScript can access each one.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Create a Money Function
Contents.Contents:
Display Money Consistently

A POS application displays money many times.

We could repeatedly write formatting code, but that would make our program repetitive.

Instead, we can create a function.

function money(value) {
  return "₱" + Number(value).toFixed(2);
}

What Does the Function Do?

It accepts a value and returns a formatted Philippine peso amount with two decimal places.

money(85)
↓
₱85.00

Why Use Number()?

Values from some HTML inputs can arrive as text. Number() converts a value into a number so mathematical operations can be performed correctly.

What Does toFixed(2) Do?

toFixed(2) formats the number with exactly two digits after the decimal point.

85
↓
85.00

Why Is This Useful?

Now every part of the POS can use the same formatting rule.

money(price)
money(subtotal)
money(tax)
money(total)
money(change)

Try It

Create the money() function and test it with different values such as 85, 120.5, and 0. Use console.log() to inspect the returned values.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Display the Products
Contents.Contents:
Turn Product Data Into HTML

Our products array contains data, but the user cannot see it yet.

We need JavaScript to turn each product object into an HTML element.

Create a Function

function renderProducts() {
  productsEl.innerHTML = "";
}

Clearing the container first gives us a clean area to work with.

Loop Through the Products

products.forEach(
  (product, index) => {
    ...
  }
);

forEach() allows us to run code once for every item in the array.

Create the Product Element

const item =
  document.createElement("div");

Now JavaScript has created a new HTML div element in memory.

We can give it the product class:

item.className = "product";

Add the Product Content

item.innerHTML = `
  <div class="product-name">
    ${product.name}
  </div>

  <div class="product-price">
    ${money(product.price)}
  </div>

  <button class="buy" type="button">
    BUY
  </button>
`;

The expressions inside ${...} insert values from the JavaScript objects.

Add the Element to the Page

productsEl.appendChild(item);

Now the product becomes part of the visible webpage.

Try It

Build the renderProducts() function and run it. Your products should now appear in the POS interface.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Make the Buy Button Work
Contents.Contents:
Now Products Need Behavior

The product cards are visible, but clicking BUY still does nothing.

This is where event listeners return.

Find the Buy Button

item.querySelector(".buy")

This searches inside the newly created product element for its button.

Listen for Clicks

item
  .querySelector(".buy")
  .addEventListener(
    "click",
    () => addToCart(index)
  );

When the button is clicked, JavaScript calls addToCart().

Why Do We Pass index?

The index tells us which product in the products array was selected.

products[0]
↓
Burger

products[1]
↓
Pizza

So the same product-rendering function can create buttons for every product while each button still knows which item it represents.

The Flow

User clicks BUY
↓
Click event runs
↓
addToCart(index)
↓
Selected product is identified
↓
Cart changes

Try It

Connect each Buy button to addToCart(index). For now, create the function so it simply uses console.log() to show which product was selected.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Add Products to the Cart
Contents.Contents:
Build the Current Order

We now know which product the user selected.

The next step is to place it into the cart.

Find the Product

const product = products[index];

Now product refers to the selected product object.

Check Whether It Is Already in the Cart

const existing =
  cart.find(
    item => item.name === product.name
  );

If the product is already present, we should increase its quantity instead of creating another separate row.

If It Already Exists

if (existing) {
  existing.quantity++;
}

The ++ operator increases the quantity by one.

If It Does Not Exist

else {
  cart.push({
    name: product.name,
    price: product.price,
    quantity: 1
  });
}

This creates a new cart object and adds it to the array.

The Pattern

Click BUY
↓
Find product
↓
Already in cart?
├── Yes → Increase quantity
└── No → Create cart object

Try It

Implement addToCart(). Add one product several times and observe that its quantity increases rather than creating unnecessary duplicate cart entries.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Render the Cart
Contents.Contents:
Show the Current Order on the Page

Updating the cart array is not enough. The visible table must also change.

This is another job for a rendering function.

function renderCart() {
  cartEl.innerHTML = "";
}

Handle an Empty Cart

if (!cart.length) {
  cartEl.innerHTML = `
    <tr>
      <td colspan="5" class="empty">
        No items yet.
      </td>
    </tr>
  `;
}

The ! means not, so !cart.length means the cart has no items.

Render Existing Items

cart.forEach(
  (item, index) => {
    ...
  }
);

For each item, create a table row.

const row =
  document.createElement("tr");

Calculate the Item Total

const itemTotal =
  item.price * item.quantity;

Build the Row

row.innerHTML = `
  <td>${item.name}</td>
  <td>${money(item.price)}</td>
  ...
`;

After building the row, add it to the table:

cartEl.appendChild(row);

Try It

Build the cart rendering function. Add a product and make sure the table updates to display its name, price, quantity, and item total.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Change Product Quantities
Contents.Contents:
Increase and Decrease Quantities

Each cart row contains a minus button and a plus button.

These buttons should modify the item's quantity.

Create a Function

function changeQuantity(index, amount) {
  cart[index].quantity += amount;
}

The amount can be positive or negative.

changeQuantity(index, 1)
↓
Increase by one

changeQuantity(index, -1)
↓
Decrease by one

Remove Empty Items

If the quantity reaches zero, the item should be removed from the cart.

if (cart[index].quantity <= 0) {
  cart.splice(index, 1);
}

Render Again

renderCart();

Updating the data is followed by updating the visible interface.

Connect the Buttons

row
  .querySelector(".minus")
  .onclick = () =>
    changeQuantity(index, -1);

row
  .querySelector(".plus")
  .onclick = () =>
    changeQuantity(index, 1);

Try It

Connect the plus and minus buttons to changeQuantity(). Add products, increase their quantity, decrease it, and observe what happens when the quantity reaches zero.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Remove an Item
Contents.Contents:
Give the Cart a Remove Action

Sometimes the user does not want to decrease an item one step at a time. A remove button can delete the item immediately.

Create removeItem()

function removeItem(index) {
  cart.splice(index, 1);
  renderCart();
}

How splice() Works

cart.splice(index, 1);

The first value is the starting index.

The second value tells JavaScript to remove one item.

Connect the Button

row
  .querySelector(".remove")
  .onclick = () =>
    removeItem(index);

The Result

User clicks ×
↓
removeItem(index)
↓
Item removed from cart array
↓
renderCart()
↓
Table updates

Try It

Add the remove button behavior and test removing products from the cart.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Calculate the POS Totals
Contents.Contents:
Now We Need the Mathematics

The cart contains products and quantities, so we can calculate the subtotal.

Create calculateTotals()

function calculateTotals() {

  let subtotal = 0;

  cart.forEach(item => {
    subtotal +=
      item.price * item.quantity;
  });

  const tax =
    subtotal * .12;

  const total =
    subtotal + tax;

  return {
    subtotal,
    tax,
    total
  };
}

Start With Zero

let subtotal = 0;

We need a starting value before adding the item totals.

Calculate Each Item

item.price * item.quantity

For example:

₱85 × 2
↓
₱170

Add the Tax

Our learning POS uses a 12% tax rate:

const tax = subtotal * .12;

Calculate the Total

const total = subtotal + tax;

Why Return an Object?

We need three related values.

An object allows the function to return them together:

{
  subtotal,
  tax,
  total
}

This is another practical example of the objects we learned earlier.

Try It

Create calculateTotals(). Test it with an empty cart and then with several products. Use console.log(calculateTotals()) to inspect the returned object.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Display the POS Totals
Contents.Contents:
Put the Calculated Values Into the Page

Calculating totals is useful, but users need to see them.

We can create an updateTotals() function.

function updateTotals() {

  const {
    subtotal,
    tax,
    total
  } = calculateTotals();

  subtotalEl.textContent =
    money(subtotal);

  taxEl.textContent =
    money(tax);

  totalEl.textContent =
    money(total);

}

What Is This Code Doing?

First, it calls the totals function.

calculateTotals()

That returns an object.

We then take its three properties and place them into variables.

Why textContent?

We learned this technique during Sign-In.

JavaScript changes what the user sees by changing the text inside the HTML elements.

subtotalEl.textContent

taxEl.textContent

totalEl.textContent

Connect It to renderCart()

Whenever the cart changes, we should update the totals too.

renderCart();
↓
updateTotals();

Try It

Connect your totals calculation to the visible POS summary. Add and remove products and make sure the Subtotal, Tax, and Total update automatically.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Calculate Change
Contents.Contents:
Calculate the Customer's Change

The customer may enter an amount of money received from the payment input.

We need to compare that amount with the order total.

Create updateChange()

function updateChange() {

  const { total } =
    calculateTotals();

  const received =
    Number(moneyEl.value) || 0;

  const change =
    received - total;

  if (change >= 0) {
    changeEl.textContent =
      money(change);
  } else {
    changeEl.textContent =
      money(0);
  }
}

Read the Input

Number(moneyEl.value) || 0

The value from an input is treated as text, so we convert it to a number.

The || 0 gives us zero when the input does not contain a usable number.

The Formula

Money Received - Total = Change

What If the Customer Has Not Paid Enough?

We should not show a negative amount as the change.

Instead, this learning example displays zero until enough money has been entered.

Listen for Input Changes

moneyEl.addEventListener(
  "input",
  updateChange
);

Every time the user changes the money field, JavaScript recalculates the change.

Try It

Connect updateChange() to the Money Received input. Test different amounts and observe how the change changes.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Clear the Order
Contents.Contents:
Reset the Current Transaction

A POS needs a quick way to discard the current order and start again.

Our Clear button will do that.

Create clearCart()

function clearCart() {

  cart = [];
  moneyEl.value = "";
  receiptEl.value = "";

  renderCart();
}

What Happens?

cart = []
↓
Remove all cart items

moneyEl.value = ""
↓
Clear payment input

receiptEl.value = ""
↓
Clear receipt

After clearing the values, renderCart() redraws the visible order.

Connect the Button

document
  .getElementById("clear")
  .addEventListener(
    "click",
    clearCart
  );

Try It

Add several products, enter a payment amount, generate a receipt, and then click Clear. Confirm that the current transaction returns to its empty state.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Generate a Receipt
Contents.Contents:
Turn the Current Order Into Receipt Text

The Print button should generate a readable receipt from the current order.

We can create a function that builds a string.

function createReceipt() {

  const {
    subtotal,
    tax,
    total
  } = calculateTotals();

  const received =
    Number(moneyEl.value) || 0;

  const change =
    Math.max(
      0,
      received - total
    );

  let receipt =
    "============================\\n";

  receipt +=
    "          MY POS\\n";

  receipt +=
    "        SALES RECEIPT\\n";

  receipt +=
    "============================\\n\\n";

  cart.forEach(item => {

    const itemTotal =
      item.price * item.quantity;

    receipt +=
      item.name +
      " x" +
      item.quantity +
      "  " +
      money(itemTotal) +
      "\\n";
  });

  receipt +=
    "\\n----------------------------\\n";

  receipt +=
    "Subtotal:  " +
    money(subtotal) +
    "\\n";

  receipt +=
    "Tax:       " +
    money(tax) +
    "\\n";

  receipt +=
    "TOTAL:     " +
    money(total) +
    "\\n";

  receipt +=
    "Received:  " +
    money(received) +
    "\\n";

  receipt +=
    "Change:    " +
    money(change) +
    "\\n";

  receipt +=
    "----------------------------\\n\\n";

  receipt +=
    "        Thank you!\\n";

  receipt +=
    "============================";

  return receipt;
}

Why Build a String?

A receipt is simply formatted text.

Each receipt += ... adds another line to the string.

Try It

Create the receipt function and use console.log(createReceipt()) to inspect the generated text before putting it into the webpage.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Print the Receipt
Contents.Contents:
Put the Receipt Into the Interface

We already know how to create the receipt text. Now we need to place it inside the textarea.

Create printReceipt()

function printReceipt() {

  if (!cart.length) {
    alert(
      "There are no items to print."
    );
    return;
  }

  receiptEl.value =
    createReceipt();
}

Why Check the Cart First?

There is no useful receipt to generate when the order is empty.

This gives us another example of an if condition controlling program behavior.

Why Use .value?

The receipt is stored inside a <textarea>, so its text is controlled through the value property.

receiptEl.value = createReceipt();

Connect the Print Button

document
  .getElementById("print")
  .addEventListener(
    "click",
    printReceipt
  );

Try It

Add products to the cart and click Print. The generated receipt should appear inside the receipt area.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Build Checkout
Contents.Contents:
Process the Transaction

The Checkout button is the main action of the POS system.

Before declaring a checkout successful, the application should make sure there is an order and enough money has been received.

Start With the Empty Cart Check

if (!cart.length) {
  alert(
    "There are no items in the order."
  );
  return;
}

Check the Payment

const { total } =
  calculateTotals();

const received =
  Number(moneyEl.value) || 0;

if (received < total) {
  alert(
    "The money received is not enough."
  );
  return;
}

Successful Checkout

alert(
  "Checkout successful!"
);

The Logic

Checkout
↓
Is the cart empty?
├── Yes → Stop
└── No
    ↓
Is the payment enough?
├── No → Stop
└── Yes
    ↓
Checkout successful

Connect the Button

document
  .getElementById("checkout")
  .addEventListener(
    "click",
    checkout
  );

Try It

Test Checkout with an empty cart, insufficient money, and sufficient money. Observe how the conditions change the result.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Start the POS
Contents.Contents:
Run the POS Setup

The JavaScript functions now exist, but the application needs to initialize itself when the page loads.

We need to render the products and the current cart.

renderProducts();
renderCart();

Why Render Both?

The product area must be populated with the available products.

The cart must also begin in its empty state.

The Initial Flow

Page loads
↓
renderProducts()
↓
Display available products

renderCart()
↓
Display empty order
↓
Calculate initial totals

Connect the Pieces

At this point, the POS has the basic interactions:

BUY
↓
addToCart()

+/−
↓
changeQuantity()

×
↓
removeItem()

Money input
↓
updateChange()

Clear
↓
clearCart()

Print
↓
printReceipt()

Checkout
↓
checkout()

Try It

Run the complete POS JavaScript and test each control. Add products, change quantities, remove items, enter money, print the receipt, clear the order, and test checkout.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Connect Login to the POS
Contents.Contents:
Now Connect the Two Parts of the Application

This is the important integration step.

We already built Login before the POS existed. The Login success branch originally only displayed a successful message.

Now we have a POS application that should appear after successful authentication.

Our Two Main Elements

authOverlay
↓
Login and Sign-Up interface

posApp
↓
POS application

The CSS Already Supports the Switch

The POS starts hidden:

#posApp {
  display: none;
}

When the show class is added, it becomes visible:

#posApp.show {
  display: block;
}

Modify the Successful Login Branch

Find the successful Login branch from the Login lesson.

Previously, you had something similar to:

if (
  email === correctEmail &&
  password === correctPassword
) {
  loginMessage.textContent =
    "Login successful!";
}

We now need to add the code that changes which part of the application is visible.

if (
  email === correctEmail &&
  password === correctPassword
) {

  loginMessage.textContent =
    "Login successful!";

  authOverlay.classList.add(
    "hidden"
  );

  document
    .getElementById("posApp")
    .classList.add("show");
}

What Does Each Line Do?

First:

authOverlay.classList.add("hidden");

This adds the hidden class to the authentication overlay.

Our CSS says:

.auth-overlay.hidden {
  display: none;
}

So the Login and Sign-Up interface disappears.

Next:

document
  .getElementById("posApp")
  .classList.add("show");

This finds the POS container and adds the show class.

Our CSS then changes it from hidden to visible.

The Complete Connection

User submits Login
↓
Credentials are checked
↓
Correct?
↓
Yes
↓
authOverlay gets "hidden"
↓
posApp gets "show"
↓
POS appears

This Is the Part You Are Modifying

Do not replace your entire Login system with unrelated code.

Take the successful branch you already built in the Sign-In lessons and add the two visibility changes:

authOverlay.classList.add("hidden");

document
  .getElementById("posApp")
  .classList.add("show");

You are modifying the existing Login behavior so that successful authentication now leads to the POS application.

Try It

Log in with a valid account. The authentication interface should disappear and the POS application should appear. Then test an incorrect login and confirm that the POS does not open.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Understand the Complete Application Flow
Contents.Contents:
We Now Have One Continuous Project

The project is no longer just a Login example or a POS example. Both parts are connected.

Sign Up

User creates an account
↓
User object
↓
Users array
↓
localStorage

Sign In

User enters credentials
↓
Load users
↓
Find matching account
↓
Check password
↓
Successful Login

Open the POS

Successful Login
↓
Hide authOverlay
↓
Show posApp

Use the POS

Products
↓
BUY
↓
Cart
↓
Quantity
↓
Subtotal
↓
Tax
↓
Total
↓
Payment
↓
Change
↓
Checkout / Receipt

The Whole Project

HTML
↓
Creates Authentication + POS

CSS
↓
Styles Authentication + POS

JavaScript
↓
Handles Sign Up
↓
Handles Sign In
↓
Shows POS after Login
↓
Handles products
↓
Handles cart
↓
Calculates totals
↓
Handles payment
↓
Creates receipt

Why Is This Important?

This is the point where the individual lessons begin to behave like one real application.

The concepts you learned earlier are now working together:

  • IDs connect HTML to JavaScript.
  • Classes control reusable CSS styles.
  • Variables hold values.
  • Arrays store collections.
  • Objects describe individual items.
  • Functions organize behavior.
  • Events react to user actions.
  • Conditions control decisions.
  • DOM manipulation changes what appears on the page.

Important Learning Note

This POS is intentionally a learning application. The authentication system is also intentionally simplified. A production POS and authentication system would require stronger security, proper server-side storage, reliable transaction handling, and additional protections.

Try It

Test the full application from beginning to end. Create an account, sign in, confirm that the POS appears, add products, change quantities, enter payment, generate a receipt, and complete checkout. Then explain which part of the program is responsible for each stage.

Contents.Title: Final Checkpoint: Build the POS Yourself
Contents.Contents:
Now Build the POS Yourself

You have now learned how to create the POS structure, style it, and give it JavaScript behavior.

Your goal is now to rebuild the important parts yourself instead of simply copying the completed application.

Build the POS in This Order

  1. Create the posApp container.
  2. Create the two main panels.
  3. Create the Products section.
  4. Create the Current Order section.
  5. Create the cart table.
  6. Add the subtotal, tax, and total elements.
  7. Add the Money Received input and Change display.
  8. Add Clear, Print, and Checkout buttons.
  9. Add the receipt textarea.
  10. Style the POS with CSS Grid, panels, buttons, tables, and responsive rules.
  11. Create the products array using product objects.
  12. Create the cart array.
  13. Find the POS elements with getElementById().
  14. Create the money() function.
  15. Render the products.
  16. Make BUY buttons add products to the cart.
  17. Render the cart.
  18. Allow quantities to increase and decrease.
  19. Allow items to be removed.
  20. Calculate subtotal, tax, and total.
  21. Calculate change from the received money.
  22. Clear the current order.
  23. Generate and display a receipt.
  24. Validate Checkout.
  25. Initialize the POS with renderProducts() and renderCart().

Do Not Forget the Login Connection

This is one of the most important parts of the project.

Your Login system was built before the POS existed.

After you finish building the POS, return to the successful Login branch you created earlier.

Modify that successful branch so it also performs:

authOverlay.classList.add("hidden");

document
  .getElementById("posApp")
  .classList.add("show");

The first line hides the authentication interface.

The second part finds the POS container and gives it the show class.

That show class is connected to the CSS rule that makes the POS visible.

The Final Application Flow

Sign Up
↓
Create Account
↓
Save User
↓
Login
↓
Check Account
↓
Successful Login
↓
Hide authOverlay
↓
Show posApp
↓
Use POS
↓
Create Order
↓
Calculate Total
↓
Receive Payment
↓
Checkout
↓
Receipt

Things You Should Be Able to Explain

Why does the POS have its own container?

Why is posApp hidden at first?

What does adding the show class do?

Why does successful Login need to hide authOverlay?

Why are products stored as objects inside an array?

Why is the cart another array?

Why does the POS use forEach()?

What does push() do when a product is added?

What does splice() do when an item is removed?

How are subtotal, tax, and total calculated?

How is change calculated?

Why does the receipt use a string?

Why does Checkout need conditions?

How does the successful Login branch connect the authentication system to the POS?

Final Practice

Rebuild the POS from the concepts you learned. Then connect it to the Login system you already created.

Test the entire project:

  • Create a new account.
  • Log in with that account.
  • Confirm that the Login interface disappears.
  • Confirm that the POS appears.
  • Add several products.
  • Change quantities.
  • Remove an item.
  • Enter money received.
  • Generate a receipt.
  • Test Checkout with insufficient and sufficient payment.
  • Clear the order and start again.

The goal is no longer to memorize individual lines. The goal is to understand how the entire application connects:

Authentication
↓
Users
↓
Login
↓
POS
↓
Products
↓
Cart
↓
Totals
↓
Payment
↓
Receipt
